newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli hoteliers hang hopes on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israeli hoteliers hang hopes on Hebron.

text.p: Israeli tourism officials hope last week's handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule will project a more peaceful image to the world and calm the jitters of potential tourists.
"Tourists are looking for peace, quiet and stability," Avi Rosental, director of the Israel Hotel Association, told Reuters.
Israel's tourism industry was reaping a peace dividend early last year until suicide bombings by Moslem militants stopped a surge in foreign visitors.

"We feel the Hebron agreement will give back to Israel and the region some stability and security and will be a boost for tourism," Rosental said. "This will bring us back to the growth pace of the last five years of 10 percent a year."
In a sign of the changing times, Israel, the Palestinian Authority and Jordan have joined forces in the wake of the Hebron deal in an advertisement that urges Americans to visit the Holy Land.
"Peace, it's a beautiful sight to see," read the advertisment released to the media on Monday by Israel's Tourism Ministry.
A ministry spokeswoman said the advertisement would run in major U.S. newspapers and marked the first such joint initiative ever taken by the three sides.
Tourist arrivals, including cruise ship passengers, dropped eight percent to 2.3 million in 1996 compared with the previous year, the hotel association said.

The year had got off to a strong start. First-quarter arrivals were up 29 percent on the same period in 1995. But a wave of suicide bombings that killed 59 people in February and March also claimed tourism as a casualty.
In the second half of the year, tourist arrivals plunged 19 percent compared with the second half of 1995.
Israeli-Palestinian violence that erupted after the new right-wing government opened another entrance to a tourism tunnel near Moslem holy sites in East Jerusalem also scared visitors away.
"It was a year of continual problems," said Pnina Ben-David, an economist at the association.
Tourism from the United States, the main source of visitors to Israel, fell six percent to 425,000 in 1996, after a first-quarter rise of 12 percent.
Arrivals from Britain slumped by five percent to 216,000 after a first-quarter increase of five percent.
Bucking the trend, the number of German tourists rose two percent to 223,000 -- still a disappointing figure for Israeli hoteliers when taking into account a first-quarter rise of 39 percent.
Hotel industry officials hope peace will not only alleviate security concerns but foster regional tour packages that include Egypt, Jordan and perhaps Lebanon and Syria.

There are some 40,000 tourist class hotel rooms in Israel and Arab East Jerusalem at present and another 20,000 are under planning or construction -- of which half will be ready for occupancy by the year 2000, the hotel association said.
"Investment in tourism is long-term. The pace shows there is investor confidence," Rosental said.

Meanwhile, Israel is gearing up for its 50th anniversay in 1998 and an anticipated influx of visitors for celebrations that have yet to be finalised but which officials said are likely to include an exhibition highlighting the nation's achievements.
"It depends on the security situation, but I hope we will get 2.8 million visitors," said Tourism Ministry spokeswoman Orly Doron.
